What Are Common Types of Head and Brain Injuries?
Brain injuries vary widely depending on the force and type of impact involved. The
American Speech-Language-Hearing Association
classifies traumatic brain injuries as mild, moderate, or severe based on factors like loss of consciousness and neurological function.
Common types we see in brain injury cases include:
Concussions:
Mild TBIs often caused by sudden impact or whiplash.
Contusions:
Brain bruises resulting from direct trauma to the skull.
Coup-Contrecoup Injuries:
Damage occurring on both sides of the brain from forceful motion.
Diffuse Axonal Injuries:
Microscopic tears in brain tissue from violent rotation or shaking.
Penetrating Head Injuries:
Open injuries where an object pierces the skull and brain.
Each condition can present differently across physical, cognitive, and behavioral domains, and early legal guidance can help preserve both long-term health and legal rights.
Physical Symptoms
Physical symptoms of a head injury can appear immediately or develop over time, and our attorneys need documentation of these impairments to prove causation and damages in a claim.
Common physical signs may include:
Persistent headaches or pressure in the skull
Nausea, dizziness, or vomiting
Vision problems or light sensitivity
Seizures or convulsions
Loss of balance or coordination
Weakness or numbness in the limbs
A proper diagnosis is the first step, and documenting those symptoms for a legal claim is what can shape the outcome of the case.
Cognitive Symptoms

Cognitive deficits are common after a traumatic brain injury, particularly when the frontal or temporal lobes are affected, and our team often works with neuropsychologists to evaluate these impairments.
Cognitive complications may include:
Difficulty with memory or concentration
Delayed problem-solving or reasoning
Confusion or disorientation
Slowed processing speed
Difficulty understanding language or following instructions
These impairments can affect a person’s ability to return to work or live independently.
Behavioral and Emotional Symptoms
Not every brain injury symptom is visible. Many affect how a person thinks, remembers, or processes the world, and those struggles often make it harder to return to work or manage everyday life.
Behavioral and emotional symptoms may include:
Irritability or aggression
Depression or anxiety
Reduced impulse control
Social withdrawal
Lack of motivation or apathy
Mood swings or inappropriate emotional responses
These challenges often strain families and caregivers, and they are part of why comprehensive compensation and support matter so much.
What Are the Common Symptoms of a Brain Injury?

Brain injury symptoms do not follow a single timeline. Some appear the moment an accident happens, while others take days or even weeks to surface, since swelling inside the skull can build gradually before it becomes severe enough to notice. That is why doctors urge accident victims to seek an evaluation right away, even if they feel fine at the scene.

How a survivor experiences these symptoms depends on the severity and location of the injury, how quickly treatment began, and factors like age and overall health. A few warning signs deserve particular attention, since they often point to a more serious injury:
Loss of consciousness, even briefly
Slurred speech or sudden difficulty communicating
Dilation of one or both pupils
Clear fluid draining from the nose or ears
Sudden changes in sleep patterns

Any one of these signs calls for immediate medical attention. A prompt diagnosis does more than protect your health, since it also creates the medical record connecting the accident to the injury, and that record is what a
Denver brain injury lawyer
will need to build the strongest possible claim on your behalf.
What Causes Traumatic Brain Injuries?
Pursuing compensation for a traumatic brain injury in Denver starts with identifying what caused it and who is responsible, whether that is a driver, an employer, or a property owner. According to
MedlinePlus
, traumatic brain injuries are most often caused by:
Car Accidents
Motorcycle Accidents
Bicycle Accidents
Slip and Falls
Falling Objects
Explosions
Flying Debris
Construction Accidents
Violence
Military Accidents
Non-traumatic brain injuries come from different causes. These injuries may result from:
Stroke
Lack of Oxygen
Suffocation
Strangulation
Drowning
Cancer
Illness
Infection

Human error and negligence cause many traumatic brain injuries, such as a distracted driver who causes a crash resulting in a concussion. Proving that a brain injury resulted from someone else’s negligent, careless, or wrongful conduct is what allows the injured person to pursue compensation through their insurance company.
Colorado Brain Injury Statistics

Behind each of these causes is a broader pattern playing out across the state. Half a million Coloradans are currently living with a disability caused by a brain injury, and more than 5,000 are hospitalized each year. Colorado currently ranks ninth in the nation for deaths due to traumatic brain injury (TBI), according to the
Colorado Department of Human Services
, the most recent data available on the issue.

The impact is even harder on specific groups. Approximately 60% of individuals within the criminal legal system have a history of brain injury, over half of people experiencing homelessness report a history of brain injury, and 50% of people living with a brain injury will go on to receive a mental health diagnosis.

These figures show that a brain injury claim in Denver rarely happens in isolation. Behind every one of those numbers is a person whose life may be permanently altered, which is why understanding the scope of the problem matters as much as understanding any individual case.
Long-Term Effects of a Traumatic Brain Injury
A brain injury does not always resolve on a predictable timeline. According to
Johns Hopkins Medicine

, moderate and severe TBIs often require months or years of rehabilitation, and the full extent of a person’s recovery may not be known for a long time after the initial injury. Some effects become permanent, changing how a person lives day to day:
Ongoing dependence on others for daily activities like dressing, bathing, or managing medications
Reduced ability to work in the same capacity, or at all, in the years following the injury
The need for lifelong therapy, home modifications, or specialized care

Because these effects often evolve over years rather than weeks, a fair settlement must account for future medical care, long-term therapy, and the reduced earning capacity a serious brain injury can cause. Settling too early, before doctors understand the full scope of a person’s recovery, is one of the most common mistakes injured Coloradans make. This is why a
Denver brain injury lawyer
at
Dormer Harpring

works with treating physicians and, when needed, outside medical experts to project these long-term costs. Before those costs can actually be recovered, though, the party or parties responsible have to be identified.
Who Can Be Held Liable for a Brain Injury?

Brain injury cases often involve more than one responsible party, and identifying every one of them is central to recovering full compensation. Liability typically falls on whoever caused the accident through carelessness, which can include:
A distracted or negligent driver
A property owner who ignored a known hazard
An employer who failed to provide a safe environment
A manufacturer whose defective equipment caused the injury
Colorado follows a modified comparative negligence rule under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-21-111
, meaning an injured person can still recover damages as long as their share of fault stays below 50 percent, though the final award is reduced by that percentage.

Insurance companies representing the at-fault party often try to shift blame toward the injured person to limit their own payout. A thorough investigation, including police reports, witness statements, and medical documentation, helps our attorneys counter that tactic and hold every liable party accountable.
What Are the Types of Compensation in a Brain Injury Lawsuit?

Compensation for a brain injury claim depends on the type of brain injury and its severity. Damages generally include compensation for both economic and non-economic purposes. Common types of damages are as follows:
Medical expenses and medical equipment
Lost wages and loss of future earning capacity
Physical therapy and rehabilitation costs
Pain and suffering
Mental and emotional trauma
Loss of enjoyment of life
Punitive damages, in limited cases involving egregious conduct

How Long Do You Have to File a Brain Injury Claim in Colorado?

Missing Colorado’s filing deadline for a brain injury claim typically means losing the right to compensation entirely, and the deadline itself depends on how the injury happened. A car, truck, or motorcycle crash gives an injured person three years from the date of the accident to file, under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-80-101
, while most other personal injury claims, such as slip and falls, dog bites, and product liability cases, carry a shorter two-year window under
Colorado Revised Statutes Section 13-80-102

These deadlines can shift in certain situations. Claims against a government entity require formal notice within a much shorter timeframe, and the filing period may pause when the injured person is a minor. These exceptions are narrow, so they should never be assumed without speaking to a
Denver brain injury lawyer
first.
The earlier a case gets attention, the stronger it tends to be. Evidence can disappear, witnesses forget details, and insurance companies gain leverage the longer a claim sits unaddressed.

Support Groups:

Brain Injury Association of America

Talk to your doctor about which program fits your situation best. Speaking with others who understand a brain injury, whether survivors themselves or medical professionals, can help you cope with the emotional impact, live more independently, and raise awareness in your own community.

faqs.question: What is the average settlement for a traumatic brain injury?

children.text: Settlement amounts for traumatic brain injury claims vary widely, often ranging from tens of thousands of dollars for a mild concussion to several million for a catastrophic injury requiring lifetime care. There is no fixed average because settlement value depends heavily on injury severity, medical costs, and long-term care needs. Our
Denver brain injury lawyers
evaluate medical records, lost income, and future treatment projections to estimate a fair value for each individual case rather than relying on a generic number.

faqs.question: Can I recover compensation for a mild traumatic brain injury?

children.text: Yes, a mild traumatic brain injury can still support a valid compensation claim. Insurance companies often try to minimize these injuries because the damage is not always visible on imaging, but symptoms like memory loss, headaches, and mood changes can meaningfully affect daily life and work. Thorough medical documentation is key to proving the claim’s value.

faqs.question: How do you prove a traumatic brain injury?

children.text: Proving a traumatic brain injury requires medical records, expert testimony, and evidence connecting the injury directly to the accident. Imaging studies, neuropsychological evaluations, and statements from treating physicians help establish both the diagnosis and its impact on daily functioning. Witness statements and accident reports often support the causation element of the claim.

faqs.question: How long does a brain injury lawsuit take?

children.text: Most brain injury cases take several months to more than a year to resolve, depending on the severity of the injury and whether liability is disputed. Cases with clear fault and stable medical outcomes tend to settle faster, while cases involving catastrophic injuries or multiple defendants often take longer to reach a fair resolution or proceed to trial.

faqs.question: What if symptoms appear days after the accident?

children.text: Delayed symptoms are common with brain injuries and do not disqualify a claim, but they do require prompt medical attention once they appear. Swelling and internal bleeding can take time to become apparent, which is why seeking follow-up care and documenting new symptoms as they arise remains important for both your health and your legal claim. The sooner you speak with a
brain injury lawyer
after symptoms appear, the more options remain available for your case.
